newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher on NAPM, Greenspan talk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher on NAPM, Greenspan talk.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed sharply higher on Monday, boosted by a combination of fresh economic data and a news report saying Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan sees no immediate inflation threats, analysts said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 19/32 at 98-13/32. Its yield fell to 6.88 percent.

Monday's rally was triggered by a drop in the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index of business activity to 51.7 in September against 52.6 in August. The data came in weaker than expected.

But analysts said the NAPM report also had some dark spots. A strong rise in the survey's prices paid index to 51.2 in September against 47.4 in August was seen as the most negative item for the market.
The impact of that component, however, was offset by a sharp drop in the supplier deliveries index to 49.7 in September against 52.5 in the previous month.

"The supplier deliveries was the highlight of this report dropping well below the 50 level, which gave us plenty of reason to ignore the prices paid index increase," said Patrick Dimick, economist at CS First Boston.
Analysts said the NAPM suggested manufacturing continued to slow, perhaps easing pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.

A Reuters survey released on Monday showed a slim majority of U.S. economists (17 out of 32 pundits) expect the Fed to tighten monetary policy at the next meeting of its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on November 13.

"The NAPM tells me the economy is sluggish ... and that we're having limited inventory rebound and we're going to be doing about 2.0 percent (GDP) growth (in the third quarter)," said Alan Levenson, economist at UBS Securities Inc.
Analysts said the bullish NAPM was likely to underpin the market in the short-term.
"Just getting through the NAPM hurdle is just going to bring a lot of people into the market in a short-term basis," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
Still on the economic front, the market took in a 0.2 percent rise in the August leading indicators report and a 0.4 percent drop in the Redbook retail index in the four weeks of September.

The market was also spurred by a report published by the Australian Financial Review on its Internet's World Wide Web site suggesting Fed chairman Alan Greenspan did not see an inflation risk in the United States.
The report quoted Australia's Treasurer Peter Costello, after a briefing with Greenspan in Washington, as saying the U.S. Fed chairman was "very optimistic."
"He indicated to me that he saw no threats to inflation down the track," the Review quoted Costello as saying.
The report lifted prices in the long end of the curve by about 8/32 in the middle of the afternoon trading session.
"The story was all over the place ... The idea that Greenspan sees no inflation concerns suggests we might see the Fed on hold for some time," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Analysts said the afternoon buying spree sparked some short-covering throughout the yield curve and fueled a technical rally even further. "We saw some short-covering here as well," the trader said.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed off four basis points at 4.97 percent. The six-month bill rate fell four points to 5.14 percent. The year bill rate was down five points at 5.34 percent.

The two-year note closed up 4/32 at 99-30/32, yielding 6.03 percent. The five-year note traded up 10/32 at 99-30/21 to yield 6.39 percent. The ten-year note closed up 14/32 at 102-17/32, yielding 6.64 percent.
